pamphlet_excerpts: Hypothermia Prevention: Wet clothing accelerates core temperature drop even during mild sixty degree rainstorms.
Barometric Trend Tracking: Falling barometric pressure indicates incoming squall lines requiring immediate camp reinforcement.
Heat Stroke Treatment: Move overheated patients into deep shade and apply cool wet cloths immediately.
Hazard Tree Assessment: Dead overhead tree branches threaten tents during high winds and nocturnal storms.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Site Survey: Scan surrounding canopy for overhead dead branches before pitching any patrol shelter.
Step 2 - Weather Assessment: Check local barometric trends and national weather service alerts before entering wilderness.
Step 3 - First Aid Review: Check patrol medical kit supplies against anticipated wilderness trip hazards and group size.
Step 4 - Response Protocol: Establish rapid evacuation routes and primary emergency communication channels for camp staff.

pamphlet_excerpts: Durable Surface Travel: Restrict foot traffic to established rocky paths to prevent fragile alpine soil erosion.
Campfire Impact Reduction: Rely on lightweight canister stoves instead of constructing stone fire rings in wilderness.
Proper Waste Disposal: Deposit solid human waste within cat-holes dug six to eight inches deep.
Wildlife Distance Maintenance: Observe grazing wildlife from safe distances using binoculars rather than approaching animals directly.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Pre-Trip Planning: Repackage group food into reusable containers to minimize disposable plastic camp trash.
Step 2 - Campsite Positioning: Pitch patrol tents at least two hundred feet away from lakes and streams.
Step 3 - Cathole Digging: Dig individual six-inch deep cat-holes in organic soil away from camp water.
Step 4 - Final Sweep: Walk a patrol grid across the campsite to recover every micro-trash fragment.

requirements.lead_text: Show experience in camping by doing the following:
requirements.req_text: Show experience in camping by doing the following: (a) Camp for at least 20 nights at designated Scouting activities or events. One long-term camping experience of up to six consecutive nights may be applied toward this requirement. Two nights may be counted toward the total for each additional long-term camping trip. Each night must be spent either under the sky, in a tent you have pitched yourself (if a tent is provided and already set up, you do not need to pitch your own), in a hammock that is safely strung outdoors, in a lean-to, or other three-sided shelter with an open front. Nights spent in indoor lock-in events, cabin camping, hotel stays, or other covered accommodations do not count toward the 20 nights. (b) On any of these camping experiences, you must do TWO of the following, only with proper preparation and under qualified supervision. (1) Hike up a mountain, gaining at least 1,000 vertical feet. (2) Backpack, snowshoe, or cross-country ski for at least 4 miles. (3) Take a bike trip of at least 15 miles or at least four hours. (4) Take a nonmotorized trip on the water of at least four hours or 5 miles. (5) Plan and carry out an overnight snow camping experience. (6) Rappel down a rappel route of 30 feet or more. (c) On any of these camping experiences, perform a conservation project approved by the landowner or land managing agency. This can be done alone or with others.
